narrativeProgression.description: Initial question about the potential impact of changing technology on financial services access in India.

RS Sharma outlines two major barriers to financial inclusion in India: lack of formal ID and high transaction costs. He explains how India addressed these issues through Aadhaar (national ID system) and mobile connectivity.
Discussion about the role of Payment Banks (largely telecom players) in providing digital financial services at low costs, and their contribution to financial inclusion.

Discussion about security and consumer trust in digital financial services. RS Sharma highlights the biometric authentication aspects of Aadhaar and the potential of mobile devices for secure transactions.

Discussion about the future of digital financial services in India. RS Sharma emphasizes the need for simple and easy-to-use architectures for financial transactions, similar to making phone calls. He envisions increased adoption of cashless transactions, particularly in rural areas.

Discussion about the value of participating in the international process at the ITU. RS Sharma highlights India's experience and knowledge in the field of digital financial services and expresses their willingness to share it with other countries.

Hi.
And thank you very much for coming.
You're here as part of this week of meetings of the focus group for digital financial
services.
And let's talk about the perspective of India.
Huge population.
Many people who don't have access to financial services.
What do you think is going to change?
And what extent will people be able to access now that the technology is changing at a very
fast rate?
See, let me say there are two major barriers to financial inclusion.
The first is the inability to prove one's identity because many people in India do not
have formal ID documents.
And the second one is actually the cost of transactions.
What has happened is that India has the characteristics that the bottom of the pyramid
would have very low value, of course, very large volume of transactions.
So unless you make these transactions cost effective, it will not be sustainable.
So these are two major barriers.
And now of course, identity problem has been solved by Adhar, which basically has issued
thus far 950 million identities to more than 1.2 billion out of 1.2 billion population.
And the second one is that now we have the 1 billion plus mobile connections.
And mobiles could be used as a very effective instrument of transactions, which will actually
reduce the cost.
So these are two barriers which to some extent have been resolved by India.
But regulation is often held up as a barrier itself.
You are the chairman of the regulatory authority.
What for you are the main difficulties in this area?

One is the people who want to hide something and they want to do some tax because they want

Well I think it's a great effort of the digital financial services you know this group which

Of course this is my first time to participate in this but what I see is that there is a concerted
